Cyclic Quadrilateral

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: This is a picture, not a game: four corners on a circle make four triangles, and the centres of those triangles always make a rectangle.
How to play: Drag the corners A, B, C and D around the circle, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Tick the boxes to show the triangle centres, circles, lines and names.
Look for the math

Drag a corner and the four triangles change shape completely, yet their centres keep making a rectangle. The old cut-the-knot page called this a Japanese theorem. Its live version now shows a GeoGebra sketch instead of the Java applet; the archived 2012 page really does embed CODE="CyclicQuadrilateral", and this port follows that applet and its article.

The claim on the old page

Every four corners on a circle make four triangles: ABC, ACD, ABD and BCD. The exact claim is: the incenters of the four triangles form a rectangle. An incenter is the point inside a triangle where its three angle-splitting lines meet; it is also the centre of the circle touching all three sides. The claim is one of the Japanese theorems for cyclic polygons, carved on a temple tablet in Yamagata prefecture in 1880. Tick "Incenters" and "Rectangle" to see it.

Why the corners are square

Inscribed angles that stand on the same chord are equal. In triangle BCD the angle at the incenter is 90° + ∠BDC/2; in triangle ABC it is 90° + ∠BAC/2. Because ABCD is a cyclic quadrilateral, those two angles at D and A are equal, so the four cyclic quadrilaterals in the old proof force a right angle at every corner of the incenter figure. The logic test checks all 4,845 quadrilaterals formed by choosing four of twenty equally spaced points on the circle, plus 500 random ones elsewhere: the corner angles are right to within a tiny drawing error in every case.

The radius sum and the rhombus

The tablet also records rABC + rACD = rABD + rBCD, where each r is the radius of one triangle's incircle. That identity makes the four lines through the incenters parallel to the diagonals enclose a rhombus: tick "Rhombus". Both claims hold in every tested configuration. One quirk stays faithful to the applet: for a triangle with a side shorter than about 0.32 board units, the applet's own distance routine gives up and the radius sum visibly fails. The test records this instead of hiding it.

The arc midpoints

Let P, Q, R and S be the midpoints of the arcs AB, CD, BC and AD. The page says PQ ⟂ RS, that both lines are parallel to sides of the rectangle and pass through their midpoints, and that these arc bisectors are the rhombus's diagonals. With arcs taken along the sides of the quadrilateral, the test confirms all of this. The applet uses a shortcut: it rotates a corner through half the smaller angle to the next corner. When a side spans more than half the circle, that is not the arc along the side, so the drawn lines can miss a right angle. The page's claim is true; this drawing follows the applet's shortcut, as the original did.

Try ticking all the boxes, then drag one corner so close to its neighbour that the side almost vanishes: which of the three patterns breaks first?
